a: When Jesus finished giving orders to his twelve disciples
p: Matthew ends each of Jesus' five long speeches with the same formula, an echo of Moses finishing his words.
b: This sentence closes the mission speech of chapter 10. Matthew uses nearly the same words after each of the five great speeches (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Many readers hear Moses in it: "When Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel" (Deuteronomy 32:45). Some scholars think the five speeches mirror the five books of Moses, so that Jesus teaches as a new Moses. Others think five is simply a convenient way to gather Jesus' teaching. Either way the formula marks a turning point: from here Matthew shows how Israel responds to Jesus' words and deeds.
orig: ὅτε ἐτέλεσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (hote etelesen ho Iēsous)

a: in prison
p: Josephus says Herod Antipas held John at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea, and killed him there.
b: Matthew already told of John's arrest (4:12) and will tell of his death (14:3–12). The Jewish historian Josephus adds that Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, feared John's influence with the crowds and had him held and executed at Machaerus, a palace fortress on a hill east of the Dead Sea (Antiquities 18.116–119). Prisoners in the ancient world often depended on friends to bring food and news, which explains how John's disciples could visit him and carry his question.

a: the Messiah's works
p: Matthew, not John, calls them "the Messiah's works." The same word returns at 11:19.
b: The narrator uses the title "the Messiah" (ho Christos, the anointed king Israel hoped for) here, while John only asks a question. The "works" are the healings and teaching of chapters 5–9. Matthew frames the section with the same word: it begins with "the Messiah's works" and ends with wisdom "proved right by the things she does," literally "by her works" (11:19). Many scholars think the echo is deliberate: Jesus' works are the works of God's Wisdom.
orig: τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Χριστοῦ (ta erga tou Christou)

a: the Coming One
p: John had announced "the one coming after me." Readers have long asked whether he now doubted.
b: John had said a stronger one was coming after him, who would burn the chaff (3:11–12). "The Coming One" may recall "the one who comes in the LORD's name" (Psalm 118:26) and the messenger of Malachi 3:1. Why he asks is debated. (1) Real doubt: Jesus was healing, not judging, and John was still in prison. Most modern commentators read it this way. (2) For his disciples: many church fathers, such as Chrysostom, held that John knew, and sent his followers so that they would see for themselves. (3) Impatience: John believed, but wanted Jesus to act openly. Jesus' answer suits the first reading: he points to the signs and gently adds a blessing on those who do not stumble.

a: The blind see again and the lame walk
t: Isaiah's signs of the new age
p: Jesus answers with Isaiah's own pictures of God's coming rescue. A Dead Sea Scroll uses the same list.
b: Each phrase echoes Isaiah: the blind see and the deaf hear, the lame leap (Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 29:18–19), the dead live (Isaiah 26:19), and good news is told to the poor (Isaiah 61:1, the passage Jesus reads in Luke 4:18). A Dead Sea Scroll known as 4Q521 (the Messianic Apocalypse) also says that in the days of God's anointed one the Lord will heal the wounded, give life to the dead and bring good news to the poor. So Jesus' answer was not vague: it used a list that some Jews of his day already linked with the Messiah. The last item, the poor hearing good news, comes last on purpose: it is the climax.
r: Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 29:18–19; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18–19; Luke 7:22; 8:1–9:34

a: People with skin disease
p: The Greek lepros covered many skin conditions, not only the disease we call leprosy today.
b: Lepros is the Greek word the Septuagint used for Hebrew tsara'at, a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean (Leviticus 13–14). Modern leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a different illness, and it is not clear it was even present in Israel in the time of Moses. So the site says "skin disease" here, as in Leviticus. "Made clean" is the language of purity: the person could go back to worship and to community life.

a: tripped up
p: The Greek verb pictures stumbling over something in the road. Matthew uses it often.
b: Skandalizō comes from skandalon, a trap or a stone that trips a walker (our word "scandal" comes from it). To be "tripped up because of me" is to take offense at Jesus and fall away. The word returns when the seed on rocky ground "trips and falls" in hard times (13:21), when the people of Nazareth "were tripped up by him" (13:57), and when the disciples desert him (26:31). Isaiah calls the LORD himself "a rock they trip over" (Isaiah 8:14), a verse the church later applied to Jesus (1 Peter 2:8).

a: A reed that the wind shakes?
p: Reeds grew along the Jordan. A scholar has suggested Jesus also poked fun at Herod Antipas.
b: Reeds lined the Jordan where John baptized, so the picture is natural: no one walked into the wilderness to watch grass bend in the wind. John was not a man who bent. Gerd Theissen pointed out that Herod Antipas put a reed on the first coins he minted at Tiberias, and suggested the crowd would hear a jab at the ruler who imprisoned John: Herod bends with every wind; John does not. The idea is attractive but cannot be proved, and many commentators treat it as possible only.

a: the houses of kings
p: John wore camel's hair. Courtiers in Herod's palaces wore fine, soft robes.
b: Matthew already described John's rough clothing of camel's hair and leather belt (3:4), the dress of a prophet like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Zechariah 13:4). "Soft" clothes were fine wool or linen worn by people at court. Herod Antipas had palaces at Sepphoris and Tiberias, and John was locked in another of Herod's palace fortresses. The irony is sharp: the man in rough clothes is now in a king's house, but as a prisoner.

a: Look, I am sending my messenger before your face
p: The quotation blends Malachi 3:1 with Exodus 23:20 and changes "before me" to "before your face."
b: In Malachi 3:1 the LORD says he sends his messenger to clear the way "before me." Exodus 23:20 has God sending an angel (the same Greek word, angelos, means messenger) ahead of Israel: "Here, I am sending an angel in front of you" (Exodus 23:20). Matthew's form joins the two and speaks to "you," so that the messenger prepares the way of someone other than the speaker. Christians read this as God speaking to Jesus: John prepares Jesus' way, and Jesus' coming is God's own coming. Mark 1:2 and Luke 7:27 use the same blended form, which suggests it was already a fixed early Christian testimony.
r: Malachi 3:1; Exodus 23:20; Malachi 4:5–6; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27; Isaiah 40:3
orig: ἀποστέλλω τὸν ἄγγελόν μου πρὸ προσώπου σου

a: the smallest one in the kingdom of heaven
p: John is the greatest human being so far, yet the least in the kingdom is greater. Who is meant?
b: The Greek is a comparative, "the lesser one." (1) Most readers take it as any member of the kingdom: John stands on the line between the old age and the new, and even the humblest disciple who sees the kingdom arrive has a greater privilege than he had (13:16–17). This says nothing about John's own salvation (8:11). (2) Some church fathers, including Chrysostom, read "the lesser one" as Jesus himself, younger than John and thought less of by many, but greater. Most modern scholars think the first reading fits Matthew best.

a: the kingdom of heaven is under violent attack, and violent people are grabbing at it
p: The Greek verb can mean "suffers violence" or "forces its way." The second half is just as debated.
b: Biazetai can be passive ("is treated with violence") or middle ("forces its way, advances with power"). Biastai are "violent people," and harpazousin means "snatch, seize, plunder." Readings: (1) Hostile: the kingdom is attacked, as John's arrest shows, by people who try to seize or crush it, whether Herod, Jesus' opponents or zealots who want to bring it in by force. Most modern commentators hold this. (2) Positive: the kingdom forces its way forward (the NIV of 1984), and eager people take hold of it with determination. Many church fathers read it this way, and Luke's saying fits it: "everyone is pressing their way into it" (Luke 16:16). (3) Mixed: the kingdom advances powerfully, and violent people oppose it. The Plain follows (1) but the Greek allows the others.
orig: ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν βιάζεται, καὶ βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν

a: For all the prophets, and the Law too, prophesied up until John.
p: Matthew puts the prophets first and says even the Law prophesied. John marks the turn of the ages.
b: The usual order is "the Law and the Prophets" (5:17; 7:12), but here the prophets come first and the Law, too, is said to have "prophesied." For Matthew the whole of Scripture points forward to the time of fulfillment. John is the hinge: he belongs to the time of promise, yet he points to the one who fulfills it (5:17–18). Luke's version says "The Law and the Prophets lasted until John" (Luke 16:16).
orig: πάντες γὰρ οἱ προφῆται καὶ ὁ νόμος ἕως Ἰωάννου ἐπροφήτευσαν

a: John himself is Elijah
p: Malachi promised Elijah before the day of the LORD. Jesus says John fills that role.
b: Malachi 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew) promises that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD, to turn hearts. Jewish hope kept this alive: Sirach 48:10 says Elijah is ready to calm God's anger and restore Jacob's tribes, and the Mishnah says Elijah will come to settle disputes (Mishnah Eduyot 8:7). Jesus says John is that Elijah, "if you are ready to receive it," because it is not obvious. In John 1:21 the Baptist denies being Elijah, probably meaning he is not Elijah returned in person. Luke 1:17 gives the key: John will "walk ahead of the Lord with Elijah's spirit and power." The church has always rejected reading this as reincarnation. Matthew returns to the point at 17:10–13.

a: like little children who sit in the town squares
p: Children played wedding and funeral in the marketplace. This generation would join neither game.
b: The town square (agora) was the open space where people traded, met and where children played. One group plays the flute for a wedding dance; another wails as at a funeral. The other children refuse both games. The point (11:18–19): John came with funeral seriousness, fasting, and they called him possessed; Jesus came with wedding joy, feasting with sinners, and they called him a glutton. Readers differ on who the complaining children are. Most think they stand for "this generation" that demands its own tune. Some think the pipers are John and Jesus, calling to a people who will not answer.

a: He overeats and he is a heavy wine drinker
p: The insult echoes the charge against a rebellious son in Deuteronomy, who was to be stoned.
b: Deuteronomy 21:20 tells parents to bring a rebellious son to the elders and say, "He is a glutton and a drunkard." The law ends with his death. Many scholars hear that charge here: Jesus' critics paint him as a rebellious son of Israel who deserves the law's penalty. Proverbs warns against the same pair: "the drunkard and the glutton lose everything they have" (Proverbs 23:21). The charge is a sign of a real habit: Jesus ate at many tables, with tax collectors and sinners (9:10–13). That a hostile saying was kept by the church is one reason historians think it goes back to Jesus' lifetime.

a: But wisdom is proved right
p: Matthew says "by her works"; Luke says "by all her children." Matthew seems to identify Jesus with Wisdom.
b: In Proverbs, Wisdom is pictured as a woman who calls out in the street and invites people to her banquet (Proverbs 1:20; Proverbs 9:1–6). Here wisdom is "proved right" (edikaiōthē), shown to be in the right. Luke has "by all her children" (Luke 7:35): the people who accept John and Jesus. Matthew has "by her works," which points back to "the Messiah's works" in 11:2. So many scholars think Matthew presents Jesus as God's Wisdom in person, a theme that returns in 11:28–30 and 23:34–37. Others read "wisdom" more simply as God's wise plan, which the results of John's and Jesus' ministries will vindicate. Later copyists brought Matthew into line with Luke (see the variant).
r: 11:2; 11:28–30; 23:34–37; Luke 7:35; Luke 11:49; Proverbs 1:20–33; Proverbs 8:1–36; Proverbs 9:1–6; 1 Corinthians 1:24

a: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
p: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum lay close together at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.
b: Chorazin is identified with the ruins of Korazim, on a hill about 2 miles (3 km) north of Capernaum, where a black basalt synagogue of the 200s–400s AD has been excavated. Bethsaida ("house of fishing") lay near where the Jordan enters the lake. Its exact site is debated between et-Tell and el-Araj. Capernaum was Jesus' base (4:13). The Gospels tell of no miracles at Chorazin at all, a reminder that they record only a small part of what Jesus did (John 21:25). "Woe" is a prophet's cry of grief and warning, not a curse.

a: Tyre and Sidon
t: Pagan cities that would have repented
p: The prophets condemned Tyre and Sidon for pride. Jesus says they would have done better than Galilee.
b: Tyre and Sidon were the great Phoenician ports to the north, the targets of prophetic judgment for their pride and wealth (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28; Amos 1:9–10). Jesus' hearers would expect them to come off badly. Instead he says they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes, the clothing of mourning and repentance (Jonah 3:6). The shock lies in the comparison: privilege brings greater responsibility. Matthew later tells of a Canaanite woman from that region who shows great faith (15:21–28).

a: And you, Capernaum
t: Capernaum and the king of Babylon
p: The words echo Isaiah's taunt over the king of Babylon, who wanted to climb to heaven but fell to Sheol.
b: In Isaiah 14:13–15 the king of Babylon says to himself, "I will go up into the heavens" (Isaiah 14:13), but he is brought down to Sheol, the pit. Capernaum, Jesus' own town, is pictured in the same way. Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead; here it stands for disgrace and judgment, not a detailed map of the afterlife. Jesus' point is that the town that saw most of his works, and was proud of it, is in the most danger.

a: Sodom
p: Sodom was the byword for a city judged by God. Jesus says it would have repented.
b: Sodom was destroyed with fire and sulfur (Genesis 19:24) and became the standard example of judgment (Isaiah 1:9–10; Jude 7). Ezekiel names its sins as pride, plenty and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49). Jesus already used Sodom in the mission speech (10:15). To say that Sodom would have repented if it had seen his works is the strongest way he could warn the towns of Galilee.

a: I openly thank you
p: The verb means to acknowledge openly. It is used for confession of sins and for public praise of God.
b: Exomologoumai means "I say openly, I acknowledge." In 3:6 it is used of confessing sins. In the Septuagint it often renders the Hebrew verb for giving thanks and praise to God (as in the Psalms). Here it is a prayer of grateful praise. "Lord of heaven and earth" echoes Jewish prayer, like Melchizedek's "God Most High, maker of heaven and earth" (Genesis 14:19). The "little children" (nēpioi) are infants, people with no learning or status, set against the "wise and clever," probably the scribes who rejected Jesus.

a: Only the Father truly knows the Son
t: A saying that sounds like John
p: This verse sounds so much like the Gospel of John that a scholar called it a "thunderbolt from the Johannine sky."
b: Jesus speaks of "the Son" and "the Father" in an absolute way, as in John 3:35; 10:15. Because the saying appears in both Matthew and Luke (Luke 10:22), many scholars place it in the early source they share (often called Q), which shows that high claims about Jesus were not invented late. Critical scholars debate whether Jesus himself said it or the early church shaped it. Readers in the 100s already argued over it: Irenaeus complained that some teachers reversed its order to claim that no one knew the true Father before Jesus (Against Heresies 4.6.1). In the 300s, Arians and Nicenes both appealed to "handed over to me."
orig: οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ

a: Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down
p: Jesus speaks as Wisdom spoke in Sirach: come to me, take the yoke, find rest.
b: Sirach, a Jewish book of about 180 BC (in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles), ends with Wisdom's teacher calling: "Draw near to me, you who are untaught"; "put your neck under her yoke"; "see that I have labored little and found much rest" (Sirach 51:23–27). Proverbs 9:5 has Wisdom say, "Come, have some of my bread." Jesus' call uses the same pattern, but where the teacher points to Wisdom, Jesus says "Come to me." "Loaded down" (pephortismenoi) is the verb Jesus uses for the scribes' heavy loads in 23:4.

a: Lift my yoke onto yourselves
p: Rabbis spoke of taking on "the yoke of the kingdom of heaven" and "the yoke of the commandments."
b: A yoke joined working animals to a plow, and in Jewish speech it stood for obedience. The Mishnah says that saying the Shema means taking on "the yoke of the kingdom of heaven," and after it "the yoke of the commandments" (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). It also says that whoever takes on "the yoke of the Torah" is freed from the yoke of government and worldly cares (Mishnah Avot 3:5). Jesus' hearers knew this language. He offers his own yoke, his teaching, as a way of life with God. The yoke is "kind" (chrēstos) not because it asks little, for Jesus asks more than the scribes (5:20), but because it is given by one who is gentle.

a: And you will find rest for your souls.
p: These words come from Jeremiah 6:16, and they lead straight into two Sabbath stories.
b: Jeremiah 6:16 calls Israel to ask for "the ancient paths" and "find rest for your souls," and the people answer, "We will not walk in it." "Gentle" (praus) recalls the king who comes "gentle and riding on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9, quoted in Matthew 21:5) and Moses, "very humble" (Numbers 12:3). Matthew places this promise of rest just before two stories about the Sabbath, the day of rest (12:1–14). Many commentators think the order is deliberate: Jesus himself gives the rest the Sabbath points to.

a: they started pulling off heads of grain and eating them
p: The Torah allowed hungry travelers to pick grain by hand. The question was whether it counted as work on the Sabbath.
b: Deuteronomy 23:25 says, "you may pick the heads of grain with your hand," so the disciples were not stealing. The issue was the day. The Torah forbids work on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10; Exodus 31:14) but does not define it. Jewish teachers listed kinds of work; the Mishnah's list of thirty-nine main kinds includes reaping and threshing (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). Pulling off heads of grain and rubbing them (Luke 6:1) could count as both. That list was written down about AD 200, so we cannot be sure how strict every Pharisee was in Jesus' day, but some groups were stricter still (the Damascus Document, CD 10–11).

a: The Pharisees
p: A popular Jewish movement devoted to keeping the Torah carefully in daily life, including the Sabbath.
b: The Pharisees (perhaps "separated ones") were a lay movement, not priests. Josephus says they handed on traditions "from the fathers" not written in the law of Moses and were respected by ordinary people (Antiquities 13.297–298; 18.12–15). They wanted all Israel to live in holiness, so the Sabbath, purity and tithes mattered to them. They were not of one mind: the schools of Hillel and Shammai argued over many rules. In Matthew they are Jesus' main opponents, partly because after AD 70 their heirs led the synagogues Matthew's community was arguing with. Modern Jewish and Christian scholars (E. P. Sanders, Amy-Jill Levine) warn against treating them as hypocrites by definition. Here their question is a real legal one.

a: the Presence Bread
p: Jesus points to 1 Samuel 21, where David and his men ate the bread only priests could eat.
b: Twelve loaves were set before the LORD every Sabbath and then eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). When David fled from Saul, the priest at Nob gave him this bread: "The only bread on hand was the Presence Bread" (1 Samuel 21:6). Jesus argues from a precedent in Scripture, and from a lesser case to a greater one, a common Jewish style: if David's need overrode a temple rule, the need of the Son of David's followers can too. Mark 2:26 names the high priest as Abiathar, though 1 Samuel 21 names his father Ahimelech; Matthew and Luke leave the name out. Later rabbis also discussed David's act (Bavli Menachot 95b).

a: the priests in the temple treat the Sabbath as common
p: The Torah itself ordered extra offerings on the Sabbath, so priests worked hardest on that day.
b: Numbers 28:9–10 orders two extra lambs every Sabbath, and the priests also changed the Presence Bread every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8); the Mishnah says the baking itself was done beforehand (Mishnah Menachot 11:2). Jewish teachers agreed that temple service overrides the Sabbath: the Mishnah lists parts of the Passover offering that may be done even when Passover falls on a Sabbath (Mishnah Pesachim 6:1). "Treat as common" (bebēloō, profane) is a strong word, the opposite of keeping the day holy (Exodus 31:14). Jesus' point is that the law itself shows that some duties outrank Sabbath rest.

a: than the temple
p: The Greek says "something greater," not "someone greater." What is it?
b: Meizon is neuter: "a greater thing." The KJV's "one greater" follows a later reading (see the variant). The same neuter returns in "something greater than Jonah ... than Solomon" (12:41–42). Readers ask what the greater thing is: (1) Jesus himself, spoken of indirectly, the view of most commentators; (2) the kingdom of God now arriving in Jesus' ministry; (3) mercy, which God wants more than sacrifice (12:7). In Matthew these belong together. For Jews after AD 70, when the temple lay in ruins, the claim had special force.

a: Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice
p: Matthew alone has Jesus quote Hosea 6:6, and he does it twice.
b: Hosea 6:6 says God desires hesed (loyal love) rather than sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. In Hebrew style "not this but that" often means "this more than that": Hosea did not reject sacrifice but put it in second place. Jesus quotes it at 9:13, for eating with sinners, and here, for the hungry disciples. Rabbinic tradition used the same verse after the temple fell: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai is said to have comforted a student with it, teaching that deeds of loving-kindness make atonement now (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4). Matthew's Jesus makes mercy the key to reading the whole law.

a: the Son of Man
p: Mark first has a saying that the Sabbath was made for people. Matthew leaves it out and stresses Jesus' authority.
b: In Mark 2:27–28 Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath, and so the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. Some scholars think "son of man" there first meant "a human being" in general (as in Aramaic). Matthew drops the first line, so here the title clearly points to Jesus. Readers differ on what follows. Many Christians read it as Jesus fulfilling or moving beyond the Sabbath (compare Colossians 2:16–17). Others, including Seventh-day Adventists, read it as Jesus claiming the Sabbath as his own day and showing how to keep it rightly, not abolishing it. Jewish readers note that Jesus' arguments here are inside a Jewish debate about how, not whether, to keep the day.

a: Is it allowed to heal on the Sabbath?
p: Jewish law let people save a life on the Sabbath. A withered hand was no danger to life.
b: The rule that danger to life overrides the Sabbath is old: the Mishnah says any doubt about danger to life overrides it (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), and 1 Maccabees 2:39–41 tells how pious Jews decided to defend themselves on the Sabbath rather than all die. The question is about a case with no danger: a withered, perhaps paralyzed, hand that could wait until the next day. Later rabbis allowed some treatment and forbade other kinds. Jesus heals with a word, without any work at all, which made it hard to charge him with breaking the law.

a: Won't he grab it and pull it out?
p: Jesus assumes his hearers would rescue a sheep. A stricter Jewish group said not to.
b: The Damascus Document, a rule book of a strict Jewish group linked to the Dead Sea Scrolls, says that if an animal falls into a pit or a cistern, no one should lift it out on the Sabbath (CD 11:13–14). Later rabbis allowed a person to bring cushions or food so the animal could survive or climb out (Bavli Shabbat 128b). Jesus speaks as if his hearers would of course help their one sheep. The argument goes from the lesser to the greater: if a sheep, how much more a human being. So Jesus is arguing inside the Jewish debate about the Sabbath, not against the Sabbath itself.

a: looking for a way to destroy him
p: This is the first time Matthew says Jesus' opponents planned his death. Historians ask how likely it is.
b: In Mark 3:6 the Pharisees plot with the Herodians; Matthew names only the Pharisees. Historians such as E. P. Sanders doubt that Pharisees would seek someone's death over a healing done with a word, and note that in the passion story the chief priests, not the Pharisees, act against Jesus. Others think Matthew is telescoping a growing hostility. Matthew writes at a time of bitter conflict between his community and the synagogue leaders who were heirs of the Pharisees. Readers should not take the verse as a judgment on Jews as a people, a misuse that has a long and painful history.

a: He gave them strict orders not to make him public
p: Jesus often tells people not to spread the word. Matthew explains it with Isaiah's servant who does not shout.
b: Scholars have called this the "messianic secret," especially in Mark. Explanations include: Jesus wanted to avoid a political uprising around a Messiah-king; he wanted to avoid crowds that came only for miracles; he wanted his identity understood through the cross. Matthew gives his own reason at once: Jesus fulfills Isaiah's servant who "will not argue" and "will not shout" (12:19). His quiet withdrawal is not weakness but the servant's way.

a: Look: my servant, whom I chose
p: Matthew's longest quotation, Isaiah 42:1–4, follows neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament exactly.
b: In the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament made before Jesus, Isaiah 42:1 names the servant as "Jacob" and "Israel." The Hebrew does not, and neither does Matthew. Matthew has "my beloved" where Hebrew has "my chosen," which recalls the voice at Jesus' baptism, "This is my dearly loved Son; in him I take delight" (3:17). "I will place my Spirit on him" fits the Spirit coming on Jesus (3:16). Jewish interpreters read the servant of Isaiah 40–55 as Israel, or a faithful remnant, or a prophet; the Targum of Isaiah reads 42:1 of the Messiah. Christians from the start read these songs of Jesus. Quotations in Matthew are translated from Matthew's Greek; the site's Isaiah will follow the Hebrew.

a: a crushed reed
t: A crushed reed, a smoking wick
p: The servant does not finish off the weak. The pictures fit the sick and the poor Jesus has just healed.
b: A reed with a crack is useless and is usually snapped and thrown away. A linen wick that only smokes is about to go out and is usually pinched off. The servant does neither: he protects what is nearly broken. In Matthew the picture fits the crowds Jesus heals (12:15) and the "worn out and loaded down" (11:28). The servant is gentle without being weak: he keeps going "until he leads justice on to victory." The last words differ from Isaiah's Hebrew, "He will truly bring justice out" (Isaiah 42:3).

a: And the nations will hope in his name.
p: Matthew follows the Greek Old Testament here. The Hebrew says the coastlands wait for his teaching.
b: Isaiah 42:4 in Hebrew ends, "The islands are waiting for his teaching" (Isaiah 42:4), where "teaching" is Hebrew torah, teaching. The Septuagint has "and the nations will hope in his name," and Matthew follows it. The nations (ethnē, also "Gentiles") appear twice in the quotation (12:18, 21). Matthew is preparing his readers for the mission to all nations (28:19), even while Jesus' own ministry is still among Israel (10:5–6; 15:24).

a: This man can't be the Son of David, can he?
p: The Greek question expects "no," but leaves the door open: the crowd is wondering.
b: Mēti introduces a question that expects a negative answer, yet hesitates. The crowd half dares to think it. "Son of David" was a title for the coming king from David's line: the Psalms of Solomon, a Jewish book from about 50 BC, prays, "Raise up for them their king, the son of David" (Psalms of Solomon 17:21). Matthew uses the title more than any other Gospel, often in the mouths of the sick and outsiders (9:27; 15:22; 20:30–31), and the Pharisees answer the crowd's hope at once with an accusation.
orig: μήτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς Δαυίδ

a: the ruler of the demons
p: The name goes back to Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, and to a Canaanite title, "Baal the Prince."
b: In 2 Kings 1:2 King Ahaziah sends to "Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron," which means "lord of the flies," probably a Hebrew mockery. Canaanite texts from Ugarit call Baal zbl, "prince" or "exalted one," so Beelzebul may mean "Baal the Prince" or "lord of the lofty house." By Jesus' day the name stood for the chief of demons, whom Jesus at once calls Satan (12:26). The "house" in 12:29 may play on the name. Latin and English Bibles followed the spelling "Beelzebub" (see the variant).

a: your own sons
p: Other Jews also drove out demons. Jesus asks why his power should be suspect if theirs is not.
b: "Sons" here means members or followers. Exorcism was known in Judaism. Josephus tells of a Jew named Eleazar who drew a demon out of a man in front of the emperor Vespasian, using a ring and spells said to come from Solomon (Antiquities 8.46–49). Tobit tells of a demon driven off and bound (Tobit 8:3), and Acts 19:13–14 mentions Jewish exorcists. Jesus' argument: if you do not charge your own people with using Beelzebul, your charge against me is unfair, and they will be witnesses against you.

a: God's Spirit
t: The Spirit, or the finger, of God
p: Luke has "by the finger of God." Both point back to the plagues of Egypt.
b: In Luke 11:20 Jesus says "by the finger of God," which echoes the Egyptian magicians: "It is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:19). Matthew has "Spirit of God," which ties the saying to the Spirit put on the servant (12:18) and to the warning about blasphemy against the Spirit (12:31–32). Most scholars think Luke's wording is older and Matthew's is his explanation. "Has already reached you" (ephthasen) means the kingdom has arrived, not just come near: the defeat of demons is a sign of God's rule breaking in now.

a: tying the strong man up
p: The picture echoes Isaiah 49: God takes the captives from the mighty one.
b: Isaiah 49:24–25 asks, "Can loot be snatched from a warrior?" and God answers that he will take the captives of the mighty and rescue them. Jesus' exorcisms show that the "strong man," Satan, has been tied up, so his "goods," the people he held, can be set free. When the tying happened is debated: at Jesus' testing in the wilderness (4:1–11), in each exorcism, or at the cross (compare Colossians 2:15). Revelation pictures Satan bound for a thousand years (Revelation 20:2), a passage read in many ways.
r: Isaiah 49:24–26; Isaiah 53:12; 4:1–11; Luke 11:21–22; Colossians 2:15; Revelation 20:2; 1 John 3:8

a: Anyone who is not on my side is against me.
p: Mark 9:40 seems to say the opposite. The two sayings answer different situations.
b: In Mark 9:40 Jesus says, "whoever is not against us is for us," about an outsider who drove out demons in his name. Here, in a dispute over whether Jesus works for Satan, there is no middle ground. "Gather" and "scatter" are shepherd words: God promises to gather his scattered flock (Ezekiel 34:12–13), and Jesus has compassion on crowds "like sheep that have no shepherd" (9:36). Whoever does not help Jesus gather Israel is working against God's gathering.
orig: ὁ μὴ συνάγων μετ' ἐμοῦ σκορπίζει

a: blasphemy against the Spirit
t: What is the sin against the Spirit?
p: In context it is calling the Spirit's work the devil's. Christians have explained it in several ways.
b: "Blasphemy" (blasphēmia) means slander or insult, here aimed at God. In context the Pharisees have looked at a clear act of God's Spirit, a man set free, and called it Satan's (12:24; Mark 3:30 says so plainly). Readings: (1) Willful rejection of known light: hardening oneself against what one knows is God's work, so that one never repents (many Reformed and evangelical writers). (2) Final impenitence: refusing God's forgiveness until death, so the sin is unforgiven because it refuses forgiveness (Augustine, Sermon 71; the Catholic Catechism 1864). (3) Apostasy: falling away after receiving the Spirit, read with Hebrews 6:4–6. Pastors of many traditions add that people who fear they have committed it show by that fear that they have not.

a: not in this age and not in the age that is coming
p: Jews spoke of "this age" and "the age to come." Jesus' words mean "never."
b: Jewish writers divided history into this present age and the age to come, when God would set the world right. "The Most High has made not one age but two," says 4 Ezra 7:50, a Jewish book from about AD 100. So "neither in this age nor in the age to come" is a strong way to say "never" (Mark 3:29 says "never has forgiveness"). Some readers, from Augustine (City of God 21.24) and Gregory the Great (Dialogues 4.39, quoted in Catechism 1031) on, also inferred from the wording that some sins can be forgiven in the age to come, a verse later cited for the Catholic teaching on purgatory. Other churches deny that the verse implies it (see Where Christians differ).

a: You can tell a tree by its fruit.
p: Jesus used the same picture against false prophets in 7:16–20.
b: In the Sermon on the Mount the image tests prophets: "it is from their fruit that you will know them" (7:20). Here it turns on the Pharisees: a good act (setting a man free) must come from a good source; calling it evil shows the speakers' own hearts. John the Baptist used the same picture (3:8–10). The point continues into 12:34–37: words, like fruit, show what a person is.

a: You offspring of vipers!
p: John the Baptist used these words first (3:7), and Jesus uses them again in 23:33.
b: Gennēmata echidnōn means "brood" or "offspring of snakes." Snakes are a picture of deceit and harm (Psalm 58:3–4; Genesis 3:1). The phrase links Jesus' preaching to John's (3:7) and looks ahead to the woes of chapter 23 (23:33). It is the harsh language of prophetic warning, aimed at particular opponents, not at the Jewish people.

a: every idle word
p: The Greek word means useless, lazy or careless: words that do nothing.
b: Argos (from "a-" not and ergon work) means idle, useless. The verse does not mean every joke will be judged, but careless words that reveal the heart, like the Pharisees' quick charge in 12:24. The idea that words will be judged is common in Jewish wisdom (Proverbs 18:21; Sirach 23:7–15) and in James 3:1–12. "Justified" (12:37) means "declared in the right" at the judgment.

a: show us a sign
p: A sign was a proof from God that a prophet's claim was true. Jesus refuses one on demand.
b: Israel's prophets sometimes gave signs (Isaiah 7:11–14; 1 Kings 13:3), and Deuteronomy warns that even a sign does not prove a prophet who leads away from God (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). The scribes and Pharisees have just seen an exorcism and explained it away, so a further sign would not help. Jesus' refusal echoes his refusal to test God in the wilderness (4:5–7). A similar demand comes in 16:1–4.

a: adulterous
p: The prophets called Israel's unfaithfulness to God "adultery."
b: The prophets pictured God as Israel's husband and unfaithfulness as adultery (Hosea 2:2–13; Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16). "Adulterous" (moichalis) here is that kind of word: a generation unfaithful to God, not a charge of sexual sin. "This generation" in Matthew means the people of Jesus' time who reject him (11:16; 23:36; 24:34).

a: Jonah spent three days and three nights
p: Jesus was buried Friday and raised Sunday. How is that "three days and three nights"?
b: The words quote Jonah 1:17 (2:1 in Hebrew and Greek), where the Greek calls the fish a kētos, a sea monster. Matthew elsewhere says "on the third day" (16:21; 17:23; 20:19). Explanations: (1) Jewish counting: part of a day counted as a whole. The Jerusalem Talmud quotes Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah (about AD 100): "a day and a night make an onah, and part of an onah is like the whole" (Shabbat 9:3). Most scholars hold this. (2) A Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion, argued by some modern writers to fit the words exactly. (3) A set phrase from Jonah, meaning a short time before rescue. Luke's version speaks only of Jonah's preaching (Luke 11:29–30); Matthew adds the resurrection.

a: the queen from the south
p: She traveled far to hear Solomon. This generation will not cross the street to hear Jesus.
b: 1 Kings 10:1 says, "The queen of Sheba heard the news about Solomon ... So she came to put him to the test with riddles." Sheba was in southern Arabia (modern Yemen), and Ethiopian tradition also claims her. Both the Ninevites and the queen were Gentiles who responded to a prophet and to wisdom, and both will "stand up" or "be raised" at the judgment as witnesses. "Something greater than Solomon," the wise son of David, fits Matthew's picture of Jesus as Son of David and as Wisdom (11:19).

a: it roams through dry country
p: Desert places were thought to be the home of demons. The story is a warning to "this generation."
b: Jewish tradition placed demons in deserts and ruins (Isaiah 13:21; Isaiah 34:14; Baruch 4:35). In Tobit the demon flees "up into the regions of Egypt," where Raphael binds it (Tobit 8:3). The short story warns that driving out evil is not enough: a life left empty is open to worse. Matthew applies it to "this evil generation" (12:45): Israel has seen demons driven out by Jesus, but if it does not welcome God's kingdom in their place, its last state will be worse.

a: his brothers
p: Christians have given three answers: younger sons of Mary, sons of Joseph, or cousins.
b: The Gospels name four brothers and mention sisters (13:55–56). (1) Sons of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus: assumed by Tertullian (about AD 200), argued by Helvidius in the 380s and by most Protestants today, since adelphos normally means brother and 1:25 says Joseph had no relations with Mary "until" Jesus was born. (2) Sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage: found in the Protevangelium of James (100s), defended by Epiphanius, and held by the Orthodox. (3) Cousins: Jerome's view in Against Helvidius, the usual Western Catholic view, since Hebrew and Aramaic used "brother" for close relatives (Genesis 13:8). Luther, Zwingli and Wesley also held Mary's lasting virginity. Mark 3:21 says his family thought he was out of his mind; Matthew omits that line.
r: 13:55–56; 1:25; Mark 3:21; Mark 3:31–35; Mark 6:3; John 7:5; Acts 1:14; Galatians 1:19; Genesis 13:8

a: my brother and my sister and my mother
p: Jesus does not reject his family, but he defines his true family by obedience to God.
b: In the ancient world family was a person's identity and security. Jesus calls his disciples his family, with "sister" added though only brothers are mentioned at the door: women are fully part of it. The idea has roots in Israel: Moses praises the Levites who put God's covenant before father and mother (Deuteronomy 33:9). "What my Father in heaven wants" echoes the Lord's Prayer (6:10). For Matthew's first readers, many of whom had lost family ties by following Jesus (10:34–37), this was a promise of a new home (19:29).

a: beside the sea
p: The "sea" is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake. Its shore and a boat made a natural theater.
b: Matthew, like Mark, calls the lake of Galilee "the sea" (thalassa), as Hebrew called it Yam Kinneret. It is about 13 miles (21 km) long. Sitting was the teacher's posture (5:1). From a boat a short way out, a speaker's voice carries well to people on a sloping shore. In 1986 a fishing boat from about the time of Jesus was found in the mud near Ginosar: about 27 feet (8 m) long, it gives an idea of the kind of boat meant. Chapter 13 is the third of Matthew's five great speeches (see 11:1).

a: parables
p: Greek parabolē means a comparison. Behind it stands the Hebrew mashal: a proverb, riddle or story.
b: Parabolē means "something set beside" another thing: a comparison. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, taunts, riddles and allegories (Ezekiel 17:2; Psalm 78:2). Jesus' parables are short stories from farming, fishing, cooking and trade that make a point about God's kingdom. Scholars once insisted each parable has one point only (Adolf Jülicher). Many now accept that some, like the sower and the weeds, have several points of contact, as Jewish parables (meshalim) about a king often did. Jesus' parables are often surprising: a crop of a hundred times, a tree from a mustard seed.
r: 13:34–35; Ezekiel 17:2; Psalm 78:2; 2 Samuel 12:1–7; Judges 9:7–15; Mark 4:2; Luke 8:4

a: some seeds landed beside the road
p: Seed was flung broadcast by hand, so some fell on paths, rocky patches and thorns.
b: A farmer carried seed in a bag or fold of his cloak and threw it in wide arcs. Paths crossed the fields, limestone lay close under the soil in places, and thorns grew at the edges. Joachim Jeremias argued that in Palestine sowing came before plowing, so the farmer sowed the path on purpose, planning to plow it in. Others reply that ancient sources show plowing both before and after sowing, so the point is uncertain. Either way the story is ordinary farm life until its ending.

a: Some gave a hundred times as much
p: A good harvest might return several times the seed. A hundred times was a sign of God's blessing.
b: Ancient writers give varied figures for grain yields, and modern estimates for Galilee are often around five to fifteen times the seed sown. A hundredfold is the yield of Isaac's field when "The LORD blessed him" (Genesis 26:12). Scholars debate whether thirty, sixty and a hundred are normal good harvests or a deliberate exaggeration. Many think the ending is meant to surprise: despite all the loss, the harvest of God's kingdom will be abundant beyond expectation.

a: the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven
p: "Mystery" in the Bible means a secret God has revealed, not a puzzle no one can solve.
b: Mystērion renders the Aramaic raz of Daniel 2, the secret of God's plan that only God can reveal (Daniel 2:18–19, 27–30). The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of God's "mysteries" made known to the righteous. "You have been given" is a passive that points to God as the giver. The disciples are not smarter than the crowd; they have been let in on what God is doing, and they keep coming back to Jesus to ask (13:10, 36).
r: Daniel 2:18–19; Daniel 2:27–30; Mark 4:11; Luke 8:10; Romans 16:25–26; 1 Corinthians 2:7–10; Ephesians 3:3–6
orig: τὰ μυστήρια τῆς βασιλείας (ta mystēria tēs basileias)

a: anyone who has something will be given more
t: More to the one who has
p: A proverb that sounds unfair. It is about understanding: those who receive will grow.
b: The same saying ends the parable of the talents (25:29) and appears in Mark 4:25 and Luke 8:18. Here it explains the parables: those who already respond to Jesus will understand more and more; those who refuse will lose even the little they had. It describes how understanding works, not how money ought to work.

a: they look, but they do not see
p: Mark says Jesus speaks in parables "so that" outsiders will not understand. Matthew says "because" they do not.
b: Mark 4:11–12 says "so that" (hina) they may look and not see, which sounds as if the parables were meant to hide the truth. Matthew has "because" (hoti): Jesus uses parables because the crowd already does not see. Readings: (1) Judgment: parables are a sign of God's judgment on a hardened people, as in Isaiah 6. (2) Mercy: parables are an invitation that tease the hearer into thinking, and only those who ask further are let in. (3) Both: the same story opens the eyes of the willing and confirms the blindness of the unwilling. Many scholars think Matthew softens Mark on purpose.

a: Isaiah's prophecy is coming true in full
p: Jesus quotes the words given to Isaiah when he was called. Matthew follows the Greek Old Testament closely.
b: In Isaiah 6 the LORD sends Isaiah with a hard message: in Hebrew he is told, "Make this people's heart fat" (Isaiah 6:10), so that they will not turn and be healed. The Septuagint, which Matthew follows almost word for word, turns this into a description: the people's heart has grown thick and they have shut their eyes. The same passage is quoted in John 12:40 and Acts 28:26–27, so the early church used it to explain why many in Israel did not believe. Jewish readers have usually read Isaiah 6 as a word for Isaiah's own generation, not for all time. Matthew's verb here, anaplēroutai, "is filled up," differs from his usual fulfillment formula.
r: Isaiah 6:9–10; John 12:39–40; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 11:8; Mark 4:12; Deuteronomy 29:4

a: many prophets and righteous people
t: What the prophets longed to see
p: The prophets looked forward to God's rescue. The disciples are seeing it happen.
b: The same idea appears in 1 Peter 1:10–12, where the prophets searched to learn the time of the Messiah's sufferings and glory, and in Hebrews 11:13, where the faithful died without receiving what was promised. A Jewish text of the time, the Psalms of Solomon, calls blessed those born in the days of the Lord's anointed, who will see the good things God brings about (Psalms of Solomon 18:6; compare 17:44). Luke 10:23–24 has "prophets and kings."

a: the evil one
p: Matthew names Satan "the evil one," the word also behind the Lord's Prayer's last request.
b: Mark 4:15 says "Satan," Luke 8:12 "the devil." Matthew's ho ponēros, "the evil one," returns in the weeds parable ("the sons of the evil one," 13:38) and is one way to read the end of the Lord's Prayer, "rescue us from the evil one" (6:13). The birds that snatch the seed are a natural picture: in Jewish writing birds sometimes stand for evil powers (Jubilees 11:11 has Mastema send birds to eat the seed).

a: When hardship or persecution comes because of the message
p: Matthew's first readers knew people who had believed with joy and then fallen away under pressure.
b: The four soils describe different hearers, and the explanation fits the church's experience after Easter. Matthew's community probably faced opposition from synagogues and from outsiders (5:10–12; 10:17–23; 24:9–13). "Trips and falls" is the same verb as in 11:6. Scholars debate whether the explanation (13:18–23) goes back to Jesus or was shaped by early preachers; its vocabulary ("the message," "persecution") is common in Acts and the letters. Either way, Matthew offers it as Jesus' own key to the story.

a: weeds
p: The weed is probably darnel, a poisonous grass that looks like wheat until it heads out.
b: Zizania (KJV "tares") is usually identified as bearded darnel (Lolium temulentum), a grass that looks almost the same as wheat while young. Its seed can carry a fungus that makes people sick. Sowing weeds in an enemy's field was a known act of spite: Roman law discusses a case of someone who sowed darnel (lolium) in another man's crop (Digest 9.2.27.14). Pulling darnel early damages wheat because their roots tangle, so farmers waited and separated the grain at harvest.

a: Leave them both to grow side by side until harvest
p: The servants want a pure field now. The master says judgment must wait.
b: The harvest is a common picture of God's judgment (Joel 3:13; Revelation 14:14–20). The parable warns against trying to separate good and evil people before God does. Christians have applied it in different ways. Augustine used it against the Donatists, who wanted a church of the pure only: the church on earth is mixed (City of God 20.9). Anabaptists answered that the field is "the world" (13:38), not the church, which should discipline its members. In 1644 Roger Williams used the parable to argue that governments must not punish people for their religion. See Where Christians differ.

a: Of all the seeds it is the tiniest
p: Mustard was the proverbial smallest seed. Botanists know smaller ones, which has raised questions.
b: Black mustard seed is about 1 millimeter across, and "small as a mustard seed" was a Jewish proverb for something tiny (17:20). Some seeds, such as orchid seeds, are smaller, and some readers have asked whether Jesus made a mistake. Most commentators answer that Jesus spoke in the language of his hearers, about seeds a Galilean farmer sowed, not as a botanist. Others say "of all the seeds" means seeds sown in a garden. The plant grows to perhaps 8–10 feet (2.5–3 m), large for a garden plant, but calling it a "tree" is a deliberate stretch (see the next note).

a: the birds of the sky come and settle in its branches
p: The words echo Daniel and Ezekiel, where birds nesting in a great tree stand for nations under a kingdom.
b: In Daniel 4:12, 21 Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom is a great tree in whose branches the birds of the sky live. In Ezekiel 17:23 God plants a cedar sprig on Israel's mountain and "birds of every kind" nest in it; Ezekiel 31:6 uses the image for Assyria. Psalm 104:12 has the birds of the heavens living by the streams. So a mustard plant that becomes a "tree" with birds in it is a picture of God's kingdom: it starts small and ends great, perhaps with the nations finding shelter in it. Some readers, mostly in the dispensational tradition, read the birds as evil (13:4, 19) and the tree as an unnatural growth of a corrupt church; most commentators do not.

a: is like yeast
p: Yeast usually stands for corruption in the Bible. Here it is a picture of the kingdom.
b: At Passover Israel removed all yeast (Exodus 12:15), and elsewhere yeast stands for evil that spreads (16:6, 11–12; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here Jesus uses it positively, a small amount hidden in dough that changes the whole batch. "Three measures" (three sata, Hebrew se'ahs) is a huge amount, perhaps 40 quarts (36 liters) of flour, enough bread for a hundred people or more, and the same amount Sarah baked for her heavenly guests: "Three measures of the best flour" (Genesis 18:6). Amy-Jill Levine notes the surprise of a woman "hiding" yeast. Dispensational readers such as C. I. Scofield read the yeast as false doctrine spreading in the church; most interpreters read it as the kingdom's hidden growth.

a: I will open my mouth in parables.
p: The words come from a psalm of Asaph. Matthew calls the psalmist a prophet.
b: Psalm 78:2 reads, "I will open my mouth in a parable. / I will bubble out riddles from ancient times" (Psalm 78:2). Matthew's first line follows the Septuagint ("in parables"); his second line is closer to the Hebrew, and his verb ereuxomai ("bubble out, pour out") is a vivid word. Asaph is called "the visionary" (2 Chronicles 29:30), so calling him a prophet is natural. The psalm retells Israel's history as a riddle with a lesson; Matthew sees Jesus' parables as bringing out what was hidden in that history. Some manuscripts add "Isaiah" (see the variant).

a: The field is the world.
p: Jesus says the field is the world. Many readers still apply the parable to the church.
b: Jesus' explanation is plain: the field is the world, and the good seed and the weeds are people. Yet the weeds are gathered "out of his kingdom" (13:41), which has led many readers to think of the community of the kingdom. Augustine read the parable as describing the church, which holds both true and false members until the end. Anabaptists such as Menno Simons stressed "the world": the church itself should be a gathered body of believers, and the parable forbids only the use of force against unbelievers. Most modern commentators think Matthew meant the world but expected the lesson to apply to his own mixed community too (compare 22:10; 25:1–13).

a: the completion of the age
p: Matthew alone uses this phrase. It ties the parables to the end of the Gospel.
b: Synteleia tou aiōnos means the bringing to completion of the present age. It appears five times in the New Testament, all in Matthew (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20), and echoes the Greek of Daniel (Daniel 12:4, 13). The last use, Jesus' promise to be with his disciples until the completion of the age (28:20), frames the whole book. The harvest is not the end of the world as destruction but the time when God's purposes are complete.

a: everyone who practices lawlessness
p: A favorite word of Matthew: those who ignore God's law, even while calling Jesus Lord.
b: Anomia, "lawlessness," appears in the Gospels only in Matthew (7:23; 13:41; 23:28; 24:12). In 7:23 it describes people who prophesied in Jesus' name but did not do his Father's will. "Everything that trips people up" (skandala) echoes Zephaniah 1:3 in some Greek texts. Matthew's concern is not legalism but faithfulness: Jesus came to fulfill the Law (5:17), and those who live as if God's will did not matter will not stand at the judgment.

a: the furnace of fire
p: Matthew uses the refrain about weeping and grinding of teeth six times. Christians read its fire in different ways.
b: "The furnace of fire" recalls Nebuchadnezzar's furnace (Daniel 3:6), and 1 Enoch also speaks of a fiery furnace for the wicked. The refrain (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30) pictures grief and rage. Readers differ on what the images teach: (1) eternal conscious punishment, the traditional view of most churches (25:46); (2) final destruction (annihilationism or conditional immortality), held by some evangelicals and by Seventh-day Adventists: the weeds are burned up; (3) hope of restoration, held by some in the early church such as Origen and by some modern theologians. All agree the images are meant to warn.

a: the righteous will blaze out like the sun
p: The words recall Daniel 12:3, where the wise shine like the sky after the resurrection.
b: Daniel 12:2–3 promises that many who sleep in the dust will awake, and the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky and the stars. Jesus' own face will shine "like the sun" at the transfiguration (17:2). The promise answers the weeds: for now the righteous grow among evil and are hard to tell apart, but at the end they will be seen for what they are. "Their Father's kingdom" is Matthew's way of saying the same kingdom from God's side (compare "his kingdom," the Son of Man's, in 13:41).

a: a treasure buried in a field
p: In a land often at war, people buried their valuables. Finders and law were an old question.
b: With no banks for ordinary people, valuables were buried in the ground (25:25). Wars left owners dead and treasure forgotten. One of the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Copper Scroll (3Q15), is a list of hiding places of treasure. The Mishnah discusses who owns things found on another's land (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2). Readers have asked whether the man acted fairly by buying the field without telling the owner. Jesus does not stop to judge it; the point is the joy that makes him sell everything. Compare the merchant in the next parable.

a: beautiful pearls
p: Pearls were among the most costly things in the Roman world, brought from the Persian Gulf and India.
b: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder says pearls held the first place among all valuable things (Natural History 9.106). They came from the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf and India, so a pearl merchant traveled far. Unlike the farmer who stumbles on treasure, the merchant is searching. Together the two parables cover both: some find the kingdom by surprise, others after long seeking, and both give up everything for it with joy.

a: sorted the good ones into containers and threw the rotten ones out
p: A dragnet catches everything. Some fish could not be eaten, by the Torah or by nature.
b: A sagēnē was a long net pulled between two boats or from the shore, sweeping up all in its path. The Sea of Galilee has over twenty kinds of fish. Fish without fins and scales, like the catfish found in the lake, were unclean under the Torah: "anything in the seas or the streams that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you" (Leviticus 11:10). Those, and dead or rotting fish, were thrown away. The parable repeats the lesson of the weeds: sorting comes at the end, and it belongs to God's angels (13:49).

a: every scribe who has learned to be a disciple of the kingdom of heaven
p: Many scholars see a self-portrait of the Gospel writer here: a Jewish scholar who follows Jesus.
b: A scribe was an expert in the Torah. Matthew is often harsh on scribes (23:2–36), but here a scribe who has become a disciple brings out "new things and old things": the Law and the Prophets together with Jesus' teaching, the old not thrown away but understood in the light of the new (5:17). Many critical scholars think this describes the author, a learned Jewish Christian, and his community's teachers (compare 23:34, "prophets, wise men and scribes"). Some have even heard a play between "made a disciple" (mathēteutheis) and Matthew's name (Maththaios). Traditional readers take it as Jesus' charge to all who teach in the church.

a: his own hometown
p: Jesus' hometown was Nazareth, a small village in the hills of lower Galilee.
b: Matthew does not name the town here, but it is Nazareth (2:23; 21:11). Excavations suggest a village of a few hundred people, with houses partly cut into the rock. The large city of Sepphoris, rebuilt by Herod Antipas, was about 4 miles (6 km) away. Luke places a longer rejection scene early in Jesus' ministry (Luke 4:16–30); Matthew and Mark place it here, after the parables. "Their synagogue" in Matthew often hints at the distance between Matthew's community and the synagogue of his day.

a: the builder's son
p: Tektōn means a craftsman who builds with wood or stone. Mark calls Jesus himself "the tektōn."
b: Tektōn is a builder or craftsman, usually in wood, sometimes in stone; "carpenter" is the traditional English. The Plain says "builder" because the word covers stone as well as wood, and in Galilee, where many houses were built of stone, a tektōn could work on buildings as well as furniture and tools. Justin Martyr (about AD 155) says Jesus made plows and yokes (Dialogue with Trypho 88). In Mark 6:3 the townspeople call Jesus "the tektōn, the son of Mary." Matthew has "the builder's son," and names Mary separately. Some scholars think Matthew wanted to avoid calling Jesus a laborer; others that "son of Mary" without a father could sound like an insult, so Matthew rephrased it. The townspeople's point is the same: they know his family, so how can he be special?
orig: ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱός (ho tou tektonos huios)

a: And his brothers are James
p: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and Judas is probably the Jude of the letter.
b: James became the leader of the Jerusalem church, "the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13), and was killed in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200). Judas is probably the Jude who wrote the letter of Jude (Jude 1:1). Matthew 27:56 names a "Mary the mother of James and Joseph" at the cross. Jerome and the Catholic tradition take her to be a different Mary, the mother of these same James and Joseph, which supports the view that they were Jesus' cousins. Others think the names are simply common and the women different. On the three views of the brothers, see the note on 12:46.
r: 12:46–50; 27:56; Mark 6:3; Mark 15:40; Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13; Jude 1:1; 1 Corinthians 15:7

a: A prophet gets honor everywhere except in his hometown
p: A saying found in all four Gospels and in the Gospel of Thomas.
b: The saying appears in Mark 6:4, Luke 4:24 and John 4:44, and in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 31), a collection of sayings from the 100s. Israel's prophets were often rejected by their own: the men of Anathoth plotted against Jeremiah, their townsman (Jeremiah 11:21), and Jesus will speak of Jerusalem killing the prophets (23:37). By calling himself a prophet Jesus places his rejection in that line.
r: Mark 6:4; Luke 4:24; John 4:44; Jeremiah 11:21; 23:29–37; Gospel of Thomas 31

a: he did not do many acts of power there
p: Mark says Jesus "could not" do any act of power there except a few healings. Matthew says he "did not do many."
b: Mark 6:5–6 says Jesus "was not able to do any act of power there," except heal a handful of sick people, and that their unbelief "astonished him." Matthew's wording is milder, and most scholars think he changed it to avoid seeming to limit Jesus' power. Both agree on the link between faith and Jesus' works: in Matthew Jesus often says "Your faith has saved you" (9:22) and praises faith (8:10; 15:28). The miracles are signs for those who are open, not proofs forced on those who refuse (compare 12:38–39).
